text:
The Daily Fix: Risk grinds higher, but lacks the conviction from players to run hot

The ASX 200, Nikkei 225 and HK50 should open on a modestly firmer footing, although it's the Nikkei that carries the stronger momentum, with consecutive gains putting the June all-time highs firmly in its sights. That being said, it could be a relatively low-energy affair today - the inputs from macro markets are broadly supportive, with a midest easing in financial conditions - notably from credit, EU govt bonds, and US real rates - providing some sort of tailwind for risk to work through Asia. 

The question is whether traders can run with the initial strength and lift equity after the initial unwind, and most importantly after the first 30 minutes of cash trade.

European bonds provide a platform for risk

European government bonds have been helpful in providing risk assets with a platform to push higher. Headlines from political leaders signalling a greater commitment to fiscal discipline have restored some confidence - or at least seeing funds covering tactical shorts in French debt, with 10-year OAT yields settling 11bp lower at 4.79% and the OAT-Bund yield spread narrowing by 10bp to 1.27%. 

That has also provided some upside for the EUR, with EURUSD taken to 1.1276, as EUR short positioning as been miodestly squeezed, although the NOK and other petro-currencies have ultimately outperformed.
The covering of shorts across OATs and BTPs has also provided modest tailwinds to US Treasuries. The US 10-year yield has fallen 3bp to 5.27%, driven predominantly by a real yields.

Crude remains a violent and whippy affair

Lower crude initially provided another tailwind for risk, although the price action has been violent and whippy, and we are effectively back to square one. Front-month Brent fell from around $101 into the $97 handle before rebounding back towards $101.

Reports of increased flows across the region have offered some downside pressure on crude, but this has been offset by varying reports around the scale of attacks on vessels moving through the Strait. For now, the market remains highly sensitive to headlines and geopolitical risk.

US equities push higher, but conviction remains questionable

US equities provide Asia with a positive lead, with the S&P 500 closing 0.65% higher and the Nasdaq gaining 0.5%. Participation, however, was relatively subdued, with S&P cash volumes around 8% below the 30-day average and S&P futures volumes around 14% below average. We have seen fresh all-time highs in both Nasdaq cash and futures, while breadth has been constructive, with 67% of S&P 500 stocks closing higher. The technical picture continues to show progression to the upside as positioning builds into earnings.

That said, this still doesn't feel like a particularly strong or convicted move on the day. Given the decline in Treasury yields, lower cross-assewt volatility and a healthy 7bp narrowing in high-yield credit spreads, one might have expected a more forceful and convicted response from ewquity, crypto, and gold. 

AI remains the dominant bottom-up story

There have been some interesting bottom-up equity developments, with AMD highlighting very strong chip demand, while Alphabet's agreement to buy power from Constellation Energy has provided another positive impulse for the AI infrastructure theme. The Magnificent Seven index has pushed to fresh all-time highs, with AMD also trading at record levels. Yet the price action at these levels doesn't look especially convincing, and the bulls may need to step up again and inject some genuine vigour if this trend is to accelerate.

Memory has underperformed, while software has posted strong relative gains against semiconductors, highlighting some interesting rotation beneath the index level.

The focus turns to the Fed and Treasury supply

The broader tailwinds remain supportive for Asia, although China remains offline for Golden Week. Attention then turns to the Fed meeting minutes tonight and a $39bn US 10-year Treasury auction. The auction could prove particularly important in shaping the demand narrative around US duration and may inject some intraday volatility into rates, bonds and broader risk markets.

Good luck to all.

text:
BUDGET 2027, THE "HIGHLIGHTS"
The 34th's second Budget renames existing schemes and shuffles existing money around without any meaningful improvement for most Irish people in real terms.

The Government boasts of a €9B surplus. But strip out exceptional corporation-tax receipts and the picture changes dramatically: the State has an underlying deficit of approximately €10.8B, with the Central Bank projecting an underlying deficit of approximately €7.9B in 2027. The headline surplus therefore gives a profoundly misleading impression of the underlying health of the State's finances.

Around 1.5 million workers do not qualify for the full €750 tax benefit trumpeted by the Government. Many will receive less than €250 a year, the equivalent of approximately €5 a week. An insulting return for working people. USC remains.

Farming, fisheries and associated contractors and hauliers remain worse off in real terms.

And apparently we have "full employment". Really? The unemployment rate is 5%, with approximately 149,500 people unemployed. The Live Register contains approximately 172,200 people, although that figure is not directly equivalent to unemployment.

More than 232,500 people receive disability income-support payments, while more than 174,600 receive caring payments. Illness, disability and carer schemes cost billions.

And the total Social Protection bill for 2027 is €31B.

So when we are told we have "full employment", perhaps we should ask what exactly that phrase is supposed to mean.

Changes to childcare benefits for couples are utterly inadequate.

Our elderly get €10 a week, doing little to offset the accumulated cost-of-living increases. The Fuel Allowance increases by €5, completely insufficient compared with the price shocks already experienced and those still to come.

And then there is the NGO and nonprofit sector.

The latest comprehensive analysis puts public funding of Ireland's nonprofit sector at €10.8B. Approximately €864M of that went to the Advocacy, Law and Politics subsector alone. Much of the remainder is effectively the State outsourcing the provision of health, social, housing and community services to organisations operating outside the traditional State structure.

Yet the public no longer has the transparency it once had.

Government funding for Benefacts was terminated in 2022. Benefacts had provided a centralised, searchable picture of State funding to nonprofits, including €7.7B in grants to almost 3,000 organisations in 2020. That transparency disappeared with it, and there is still no equivalent comprehensive central database.

€10.8B is an extraordinary amount of public money to be flowing through a sector for which there is no equivalent single, comprehensive public view of who receives what, from whom, and for what purpose.

International development assistance receives increased funding. 1,000 new Gardaí. Dysfunctional Tusla gets another 322 staff, taking its workforce to more than 6,250, without any apparent structural reform.

Defence spending increases by 10.5%. Data centres: nothing meaningful changes. They continue to get a free pass.

Uisce Éireann continues to receive billions for water infrastructure while Ireland's leaking and failing water system remains an enduring national embarrassment.

text:
102 years of life, nearly eight decades of acting, and a place in Hollywood history that was secured with her very first film. 🕊️

Legendary actress Eva Marie Saint has passed away at 102, dying at her Los Angeles home and leaving behind a career that seemed to touch almost every era of American screen history.

Her arrival in movies was extraordinary. Saint made her film debut opposite Marlon Brando in On the Waterfront and immediately won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress. Rather than chase every role Hollywood offered afterward, she became known for being unusually selective, even turning down major projects to prioritize her family.

Then came Alfred Hitchcock’s North by Northwest, where she transformed into the elegant and mysterious Eve Kendall opposite Cary Grant. From there, her career moved through Raintree County, Exodus, The Russians Are Coming, the Russians Are Coming, Grand Prix and Nothing in Common, before later generations discovered her as Martha Kent in Superman Returns and heard her as Katara in The Legend of Korra.

She worked with legends, became one herself, and remained active well into her 90s.

Eva Marie Saint didn’t simply survive the passing of Hollywood eras. She became a bridge between them.

Rest in peace to a true screen icon. 🤍
author: oniichanph
authorBio: Remembering the greats 💖

text:
EVA MARIA SAINT (1924 - 2026)

Eva Marie Saint, one of the last survivors of Hollywood’s golden age of the 1940s and 50s, has died aged 102. 

Her screen work spanned six decades: Saint made her screen debut opposite Marlon Brando in 'On the Waterfront', starred in Hitchcock’s celebrated thriller 'North by Northwest', and in one of her last screen appearances played Superman’s adoptive mother Martha Kent in the 2006 superhero film 'Superman Returns'.

A family spokesman said Saint had died of natural causes at her home in Los Angeles.

Born in 1924 in New Jersey to a Quaker family, Saint had an early career as a jobbing radio and TV performer.

Her early days were chronicled in a 1949 feature in Life magazine, following her struggles to get a foothold in the industry. It had the prophetic words: “Eva Marie Saint name may someday be a household word..."  

By the early 50s she was making some headway, appearing in 1953 in both the original telecast and the premiere Broadway production of the Horton Foote play 'The Trip to Bountiful'.

Saint told the Santa Barbara Independent paper that 'On the Waterfront' director Elia Kazan spotted her in 'The Trip to Bountiful' and invited her to audition by improvising a scene with Marlon Brando. 

Saint said she found the experience difficult, but was offered the role of Edie Doyle, Brando’s love interest, in the hard hitting drama about mob union activities; she would go on to win the Oscar for best supporting actress in 1955.

After this meteoric success, Saint quickly began securing a wide variety of leading roles. She starred opposite Bob Hope in 'That Certain Feeling', played a woman married to a secret drug addict in the Fred Zinnemann-directed issue picture 'A Hatful of Rain' and co-starred with Elizabeth Taylor in the period western 'Raintree County. 

Saint then achieved the highly coveted role opposite Cary Grant in Alfred Hitchcock’s 1959 spy classic 'North by Northwest': secret agent Eve Kendall, “a blond who has all the answers”. 

She said in a TCM interview that she got her career-defining role – partly – by wearing beige and white gloves to a lunch appointment with Hitchcock.

Saint kicked off the 1960s by playing American nurse Kitty Fremont in 'Exodus', a hit adaptation of Leon Uris’s novel about the creation of the state of Israel, but subsequently eased up on her workload to prioritise her young family. 

In 1962 she appeared opposite Warren Beatty in 'All Fall Down' as a woman infatuated with Beatty’s drifter, starred as Richard Burton’s wife in 'The Sandpiper' in 1965 alongside Elizabeth Taylor and played a journalist who has an affair with Yves Montand’s race driver in 'Grand Prix in 1966'.

Despite critical acclaim for her role in the 1970 infidelity drama 'Loving' alongside George Segal, Saint’s film parts largely dried up in the 70s and 80s, with the actor instead turning to TV movies and guest appearances.

Sporadic film appearances ensued after a “comeback” in the 1986 Tom Hanks/Jackie Gleason comedy 'Nothing in Common'.

Later appearances included as Sam Shepard’s mother in the Wim Wenders-directed western 'Don’t Come Knocking' in 2005, and a year later she was cast in 'Superman Returns' – where she was “reunited” with 'On the Waterfront' star Brando, whose estate gave permission for 1978 footage to be used in the film after his death in 2004.

Saint worked more consistently in TV, winning a best supporting actress Emmy award for the 1990 mini-series 'People Like Us', adapted from Dominick Dunne’s novel. Her final onscreen role was in 'Winter’s Tale' as the sister of the immortal Colin Farrell.

Saint married Jeffrey Hayden in 1951 and had two children; they remained together until his death in 2016.

text:
John Wrighten sued South Carolina in 1946 to enter a law school that would not have him, and the state built an entire separate one rather than let him through the door. Then he enrolled in that school, finished it, and had to pass a written bar exam that white graduates had been excused from since 1886.

The exemption vanished while he was still a student in the building his own lawsuit paid for. He got the door open and they took the handle off it.

In the spring of 1950, two men walked out of Orangeburg, South Carolina holding law degrees that were also law licenses. Their names were Albert A. Kennedy and Julius Thomas Williams Jr.

Neither man ever sat for a bar examination, because South Carolina did not require one of them. Under a rule the state had kept since 1886, a diploma from one of its law schools was itself admission to the bar.

That rule was sixty-four years old when Kennedy and Williams used it.

It did not survive the next twelve months.

By 1951 the diploma privilege was gone. Every law graduate in the state, white or Black, now had to pass a written examination graded by six practicing lawyers.

The privilege had been born in a room Black men were already put out of once.

South Carolina's public law school in Columbia was integrated during Reconstruction, and it was the only state university in the South that admitted and graduated Black students in those years. Between 1868 and 1876 it turned out thirty-nine lawyers, and eleven of them were Black.

The first was Walter Raleigh Jones.

On June 7, 1877, a joint resolution of the General Assembly closed the law school entirely. It reopened in 1884 for white students only, and two years after that its graduates were handed automatic admission to the bar.

The exemption arrived once there was nobody left in the building it could benefit but white men.

It stayed that way for two generations. Then a young man from Charleston started writing letters.

John Howard Wrighten came up through the Avery Normal Institute, the first accredited secondary school for Black children in Charleston. He graduated in 1943 and wrote to the College of Charleston that same year, asking what a Black applicant would have to do to be admitted.

Nothing came of it.

So in 1944 he went back to Avery and organized thirty-two seniors to do it with him. They wrote their letters as an assignment in Julia Brogdon's course, a class the school listed on its schedule as Problems in Democracy.

The College of Charleston was a municipal college then, funded by the city, which was the entire basis of the students' argument.

By that fall it was not a municipal college anymore. It had gone private, and the students were refused.

City officials offered Avery six scholarships to South Carolina State College in Orangeburg to settle the matter, which is the kind of offer that tells you the letters landed.

Wrighten served in World War II and came home the way a lot of Black veterans came home, done asking politely. On June 30, 1946, he applied to the University of South Carolina School of Law.

He was turned down on the ground of race and he sued, and the NAACP sent Thurgood Marshall to argue it. In the federal district court in Charleston, Judge J. Waties Waring held that a Black resident of the state was entitled to the same opportunity and facilities afforded to white residents for a legal education.

Waring then gave South Carolina three ways to comply.

Admit Wrighten to the law school in Columbia, or close that law school down. Or build a separate law school of substantially equal quality for Black students.

The state took the third door before the ink dried.

The General Assembly appropriated two hundred thousand dollars for a law school at South Carolina State College and thirty thousand more for its library. It opened on September 17, 1947, with nine students.

Marshall told his own client not to enroll in it. He called what the state had thrown together a Jim Crow dump in South Carolina, and he was not being unkind to the men who would teach there.

He was describing an appropriation.

In April 1950 the University of South Carolina dedicated a new home for its own law school in Columbia. That building cost two hundred and fifty thousand dollars.

The state had spent less on an entire law school for Black South Carolinians than on one building for white ones, and it had done both inside of thirty-six months.

Wrighten waited two years and enrolled at Orangeburg anyway, in September 1949. Kennedy and Williams got there ahead of him.

They finished in 1950, and because the rule still stood that spring, South Carolina handed two Black men licenses to practice law without asking either of them a single question. Then the rule was gone.

Matthew J. Perry Jr. graduated from the same school the very next year and had to sit the written examination.

He had grown up in Columbia and served in Europe as an Army sergeant. On a troop train layover in Alabama during the war he went looking for something to eat in a segregated depot.

He found Italian prisoners of war being served inside the whites-only dining room while Black American soldiers took their meals through a window.

Perry passed the bar on his first attempt. He opened an office in Spartanburg, the first Black lawyer that city had seen since the 1930s.

John Wrighten was admitted to the South Carolina bar in 1953, by examination.

The man whose lawsuit built the school did not get what the school's first graduates got. He sued a door open and the state pulled the handle off before he reached it.

A South Carolina legislator wrote to a colleague around that time that the new requirement would bar Negroes and some undesirable whites from practicing in the state. That letter was surfaced by William Hine, who taught history at South Carolina State for decades.

Hine was blunt when a reporter asked him about it in 2020, that examinations had always been a resource the white community controlled, and that the men who wrote them knew it.

Here is the part almost nobody knows.

The diploma privilege was not the only door South Carolina closed.

The state also allowed admission by reading law, the old apprenticeship route, studying in a practicing attorney's office instead of attending a school. That route was eliminated in 1957, shortly after a Black applicant used it.

South Carolina also allowed reciprocity, admitting lawyers already licensed in other states. That was abolished in January 1972, not long after a Black member of the Oklahoma bar applied under it.

Three routes into the profession, three closures, each one arriving right behind a Black man who had found the way through.

That is not a theory circulating on the internet. It is an argument four Black law graduates laid out in a federal courtroom, and it is printed in the reported decision.

Their names were David Richardson, Patrick Kelly, Hiram Spain, and Patricia King.

Richardson held a law degree from American University, Kelly and Spain from Howard, King from North Carolina Central. Every one of them had satisfied every requirement South Carolina set for admission to its bar except the examination.

They sued the Board of Law Examiners, and in 1976 the case reached the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit. They put the three dates on the table side by side and asked the court to look at them together.

The Examiners answered that the state had never written a rule explicitly barring Black lawyers, and that each change matched a national trend toward higher standards. They added that by the 1970 census South Carolina had the highest proportion of Black lawyers of any state in the country.

That proportion was three and four tenths percent.

The court ruled the evidence fell short of proving a deliberate state scheme. The pattern argument failed.

But the judges kept reading, and what they found in the grading was its own kind of testimony.

One examiner told the court his method was to take the strongest paper in the pile, work out how many points it needed to become an A, and add that same number to everyone else's score. Another explained that his own cutoff never moved, that the magic passing point is 70, and he ranged up or down from there.

Kelly's average came to 69.6 and he was failed. Spain's came to 70.5 and he was failed.

A man who averaged 69.3 was passed.

The court held the Examiners had acted arbitrarily as to Spain and Kelly, and ordered on remand that both be certified as having passed the South Carolina bar. It took two Howard-trained lawyers a federal appeal to be handed what Kennedy and Williams received in 1950 for walking across a stage.

The school in Orangeburg lasted nineteen years and graduated fifty-one people, fifty men and one woman. Its library grew from seventy-five hundred volumes to twenty-one thousand five hundred and thirty-seven.

Cassandra Maxwell, the first Black woman admitted to the South Carolina bar, taught there.

Between 1951 and 1968, twenty-nine of the fifty Black lawyers admitted to the South Carolina bar came out of that one small building.

They defended the Friendship Nine in Rock Hill. They desegregated Clemson, the University of South Carolina, and the Charleston County schools.

One graduate, Ruben Gray, described driving across the state to represent people arrested at demonstrations and getting not even gas for your car. Ernest A. Finney Jr., class of 1954, became chief justice of the South Carolina Supreme Court.

Matthew Perry became the first Black federal judge in the state. There is a federal courthouse in Columbia with his name on it now.

The law school graduated its last class on May 15, 1966, and closed.

John Wrighten practiced in Charleston for decades and later pastored African Methodist Episcopal churches in Connecticut. When he died in 1996 at seventy-five, a Charleston attorney named Russell Brown said that among Black lawyers in that state he was the granddaddy of us all.

South Carolina still has no diploma privilege.

In the summer of 2020, with a pandemic filling the hospitals, more than a hundred and fifty South Carolina law graduates petitioned their state Supreme Court to admit them without an in-person examination. The court said no and held the exam.

Almost none of the people who signed that petition knew why the privilege they were asking for did not exist.

It ended the year two Black men in Orangeburg used it, and the state has never been made to explain that. Not in a courtroom, not in a legislative session, not in one official word since.

Kennedy and Williams, then Wrighten, then Richardson and Kelly and Spain and King.

The dates are all on file, in the statute books and in the Fourth Circuit reports, and they line up the way they line up whether anyone opens them or not. Somebody ought to be reading them.

John Wrighten fought for a door that was never supposed to open for him, and the people who followed him used that opening to change the law. I share stories like his because history is built by people who challenge the limits placed in front of them.

text:
POWERFUL: #Commanders running back Rachaad White finished high school with ZERO DIVISION I OFFERS.

Not one.

White rushed for 1,325 yards as a senior but was an unranked recruit, forcing him to begin his college career at Division II Nebraska-Kearney before transferring to Mt. San Antonio College.

Life there was brutal.

White worked warehouse jobs, assembled furniture, and even worked security at Coachella just to help pay for rent and food while playing JUCO football.

At one point, he was sharing a two-bedroom apartment with roughly 15 OTHER PEOPLE.

White eventually earned his opportunity at Arizona State before Tampa Bay selected him in the THIRD ROUND of the NFL Draft.

Zero D1 offers.

D2 ➡️ JUCO ➡️ NFL.

What an unbelievable journey.

❤️

text:
The Fourth Joyful Mystery of the Rosary: The Purification of Our Lady and the Presentation of the Child Jesus in the Temple

Since the fall of our first parents, human mothers have carried in their wombs souls dead to grace and have given birth to children stained with sin. Therefore it is necessary for the waters of Baptism to confer on these infants a second life, the supernatural life. A ceremony of purification is also required for these mothers, a rite which was of obligation under the Old Law, but under the New Law remains only as a pious custom.

The Blessed Virgin was not subject to the rule of sin. By a special privilege she was preserved free from the stain of original sin and was created and conceived in the fullness of grace. Moreover, she became a mother not by any human agency but by the power of the Holy Spirit, which preserved intact her angelic virginity. For this reason Mary was not bound by the Mosaic law which laid down the ceremony of purification as necessary for all mothers. Nevertheless, in order to give us an example of humility and of absolute obedience to the law of God, she chose to fulfil this sacred rite.

How well do we comply with the law of God, with the precepts of the Church, and with the commands of our superiors who represent divine authority? Perhaps we can excuse ourselves too easily from our obligations. Perhaps we are not sufficiently ready to give good example to others. We may evade the sacrifices which our duty demands of us, or we may fail to see God in the person who gives us our instructions.

Let us learn from the Blessed Virgin. Even when she was not obliged to do so, she obeyed the law and gave us a wonderful example of humility and submission to Almighty God.

Then Joseph and Mary carried the Infant Jesus to the Temple to offer Him to God and to buy Him back as their first-born son with the price paid by the poor, namely, with a pair of turtle-doves or two young pigeons. Let us reflect on this new act of humility on the part of the Holy Family. In spite of the supreme dignity which had been accorded them, they submitted quietly to the law which bound those in poverty and in sin. We who are so fond of money and of ostentation have much to learn from this scene. Jesus, the God-Man, is purchased back as a sinner for two young pigeons. Mary, the immaculate virgin and mother, and Joseph, the holiest and noblest of men, make themselves subject to the law of sin. We can derive from this lessons in humility and in detachment.

During the ceremony a devout man, enlightened by God, entered the temple. He asked and obtained the privilege of holding the divine Infant in his arms. This was Simeon, a holy old man to whom the Holy Spirit had revealed that before he died he would see the expected Messiah, the Redeemer of the sinful human race. Overjoyed as he held Jesus in his arms, he exclaimed: “Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word, in peace.” (Luke 2:29)

May God grant that when we come to the end of our mortal lives we may also have the pleasure of clasping Jesus to our hearts. Then we can say with confidence in God’s mercy: Receive thy servant in peace, O Lord. Forgive him and receive him into everlasting happiness. (Antonio Cardinal Bacci)

text:
In his On the Incarnation, he has passages like this, which sound very much like the idea that the Word merely assumed a human body, not a full human nature:

"For He did not simply will to become embodied, or will merely to appear. For if He willed merely to appear, He was able to effect His divine appearance by some other and higher means as well. But He takes a body of our kind, and not merely so, but from a spotless and stainless virgin, knowing not a man, a body clean and in very truth pure from intercourse of men. For being Himself mighty, and Artificer of everything, He prepares the body in the Virgin as a temple unto Himself, and makes it His very own as an instrument, in it manifested, and in it dwelling. And thus taking from our bodies one of like nature, because all were under penalty of the corruption of death He gave it over to death in the stead of all, and offered it to the Father."

He never quite comes out and says that the Word took the place of the human soul in Jesus' body, but he never really says anything about that human soul either. It's not quite heresy, but it's certainly not the full orthodox position of a century later.

🚨 MARYLAND OFFERS MORE AID TO SMALL BUSINESSES BATTERED BY YEARS OF PURPLE LINE CONSTRUCTION: With the long-delayed Purple Line nearing completion, the state is again offering financial assistance to businesses that say years of road closures, blocked parking and reduced foot traffic have pushed them to the brink. 

Maryland’s Purple Line Small Business Grant Program has already distributed about $2 million to more than 180 businesses, with individual awards ranging from $5,000 to $40,000 in recent rounds. Gov. Wes Moore also proposed another $3 million for storefront and façade improvements along the corridor. 

But some owners say the assistance is too little and too late. Businesses in Silver Spring and Takoma Park have reported years of lost customers and repeated construction disruptions, with some saying they were denied grants despite operating directly in heavily affected areas. 

The accountability issue is hard to ignore: after years of delays and billions in added costs, Maryland is now spending more taxpayer money to help businesses survive the damage caused by the project itself. The Purple Line is now substantially complete, but for many small businesses, the question is whether they can stay open long enough to see trains finally begin running.

text:
Only financially retarded people think Elon becoming a trillionaire means he has a trillion dollars sitting in a bank account or something. That’s a COMPLETE MISUNDERSTANDING of how wealth works.

Net worth is the value of everything you own, minus everything you owe. Most of Elon’s wealth comes from his ownership in his companies. Those shares represent a piece of each business, and their value changes as investors put a higher or lower price on that business. He can become billions of dollars wealthier without selling a single share or receiving a dollar in cash.

Here’s a simple example... say you own 10% of a company worth $5 trillion. Your stake is valued at $500 billion. If that company’s value grows to $10 trillion and you still own the same 10%, your stake is now valued at $1 trillion. You didn’t get a $500 billion paycheck. You own the same percentage of a business that has become more valuable. Your bank balance could still be exactly the same.

That ownership is real wealth, but turning it into cash means selling shares to buyers at whatever price they’re willing to pay, with potential taxes on the gains. Selling a huge stake could also push the share price down, so you can’t assume the entire holding could be sold at the headline valuation. He can also borrow against shares, but that creates debt. None of this means he has a trillion dollars sitting in a checking account. It means the estimated value of what he owns, after subtracting what he owes, has reached that level.

Plus, just look at what his companies actually do.

SpaceX reuses rockets to lower the cost of reaching space, with the bigger goal of making life multi-planetary. The mission is to build a self-sustaining civilization beyond Earth so humanity’s entire future doesn’t depend on what happens to one planet. If something catastrophic happens here, human life, everything we’ve learned and consciousness itself could continue somewhere else. Think about how much that could mean for our kids and the generations after them.

Starlink brings internet to people and places that have struggled to get connected. Just imagine what the internet has done for YOU. What you’ve learned, the opportunities you’ve found, the people you’ve met, maybe even the business you’ve built. Now imagine finally getting that access after being cut off from it. A child can access lessons their school couldn’t offer before. A doctor in a remote community can consult a specialist hundreds of miles away. That connection can change the opportunities someone has for the rest of their life.

Tesla is helping move transportation toward electric cars while building batteries that make better use of energy. Powerwall can keep a family’s lights on during an outage and store solar energy for use after sunset. Larger batteries can support the grid and store electricity until it’s needed. These products solve problems people deal with every day, from keeping their homes powered to making their energy bills more manageable.

And FSD is a huge part of this. I use it with my family, so I see how much of the driving it already handles while I supervise it. The bigger goal is fully autonomous transportation that reduces crashes, make rides more affordable and give people time back. Think about an older person who can no longer drive, or someone whose disability keeps them from getting around on their own. Being able to get to work, see family or make a doctor’s appointment without depending on someone else could change their life.

When these companies execute, grow their businesses and give investors stronger reasons to believe in their future earnings, their value can rise. Elon benefits bc he owns a piece of them. Other shareholders benefit from the increase in the value of their shares too. And it works both ways... when those values fall, his net worth falls with them.

As an investor, I WANT the companies I own to build better products, reach more people and become more valuable. That’s why I back Elon. I’ve put everything I’ve ever made in my life behind his companies bc I believe giving people more opportunity, solving real problems and helping protect humanity’s future are worth investing in. Even knowing I could lose it all, those are missions I’m willing to put my own money behind.

If Tesla and SpaceX improve people’s lives and become more valuable doing it, Elon benefits and other shareholders, including me, can share in that success. That’s exactly the outcome I’m backing. Building things that benefit humanity and creating wealth for investors often go hand in hand. But if you look at that and picture a trillion dollars sitting in Elon’s checking account, you don’t understand basic finance. Before lecturing anyone about his wealth, learn the difference between the value of what someone owns and the cash sitting in their bank.

text:
🚨 UPDATE: New York Marine and General Insurance Company (NYM) has filed a response opposing Roc Nation’s request for permission to submit an additional sur reply in its insurance coverage lawsuit.

NYM argues that it did not raise a new ground for dismissal in its reply. Instead, the insurer says it was responding directly to arguments Roc Nation itself made in opposition, including Roc Nation’s characterization of NYM’s defense offer for Desiree Perez as merely “performative,” its claim that NYM never truly intended to fund the defense, and its accusations of a “wait and see” or “bait and switch” coverage strategy.

NYM says that because Roc Nation challenged the factual foundation of NYM’s earlier submissions, the insurer was entitled to submit additional evidence showing that its defense offer remained available and that it continued requesting information necessary to fund and coordinate Perez’s defense.

The insurer specifically points to requests allegedly made on March 23, April 1, and July 20, 2026 for information including Perez’s counsel information, post tender invoices, attorney rates, nonprivileged reporting, a litigation budget, and a defense coordination conference. NYM says counsel for Perez and Roc Nation acknowledged on August 19 that they had not provided a response to NYM’s questions and directed future communications through coverage counsel. NYM says it renewed those requests again on August 25 and September 16.

NYM also pushes back on Roc Nation’s accusation that the insurer improperly disclosed confidential defense cost information in the Florida federal action. According to NYM, its Florida filing did not reveal any specific defense cost figure and merely stated that the insureds had incurred “hundreds of thousands of dollars” in attorneys’ fees before tendering the claim. NYM argues that Roc Nation had already publicly placed the magnitude of its claimed losses at issue in the New York case.

The insurer maintains that its reply did not create a new “non cooperation” defense. It says the challenged evidence was submitted only to rebut Roc Nation’s claims about NYM’s intent and conduct after issuing its reservation of rights.

NYM is asking Justice Phaedra Perry Bond to deny Roc Nation permission to file the additional sur reply and to decline to consider Roc Nation’s proposed response and accompanying affirmation.

The judge has not yet ruled on the request.

Ted Cruz Blasts Tucker Carlson Over Hitler, WWII Remarks

Sen. Ted Cruz delivered a blistering rebuke of Tucker Carlson on Monday's "Verdict with Ted Cruz" podcast, accusing the conservative commentator of defending Adolf Hitler and Nazi Germany following Carlson's contentious interview with former British Cabinet minister Sir Jacob Rees-Mogg.

Cruz, joined by co-host Ben Ferguson, devoted a substantial portion of the podcast episode to Carlson's discussion with Rees-Mogg about Britain, World War II, and Russia — repeatedly arguing that Carlson's comments reflected a broader pattern of hostility toward America and its Western allies.

Editor’s Note: Ted Cruz’s Clarence Thomas Book #1 on Amazon, See Free Offer

"Come on, Tucker didn't go full Nazi, did he?" Cruz said sarcastically before playing audio from Carlson's interview. "I want you to give a listen to Tucker saying that he really wishes Hitler had won World War II."

Carlson did not explicitly say in the excerpt that he wished Hitler had won.

Instead, the exchange highlighted by Cruz began with Carlson questioning whether Britain had benefited from defeating Nazi Germany.

"We did the right thing," Rees-Mogg said.

"Is it a better country than it was? To have defeated Hitler, yes. So the U.K. is a better country now? It's a healthier country now?" Carlson responded.

"Otherwise, we'd be speaking German," Rees-Mogg replied.

"Who cares?" Carlson said. "There are a lot of people in Britain who can't speak English. So it would be nice to have at least a European language spoken in your country."

Rees-Mogg rejected the argument: "We want to speak English. Thanks so much."

Ferguson said he was "truly shocked" by the exchange, while Cruz cited a response he posted publicly: "Yes, Tucker. The U.K. is better off for winning World War II. America is better off for winning World War II. And the world would be much worse off if the Nazis had won World War II. This is not complicated."

The confrontation grew sharper in another clip involving Hitler's intentions toward Britain.

"Hitler did not want to go to war with the U.K.," Carlson said, later stressing that Hitler had "repeatedly" said publicly and through diplomatic channels that he did not want war with Britain.

Rees-Mogg pushed back forcefully.

"You seem to be putting more trust in Hitler than I would," he told Carlson, pointing to Hitler's broken agreements and adding, "I'm very surprised you're verging on defending Hitler."

"Yeah, I guess I'm just a secret Nazi," Carlson responded. "I'm actually not a secret Nazi."

"I'm reassured," Rees-Mogg dryly replied.

"And hardly a public Nazi," Carlson added.

Cruz seized on that exchange, accusing Carlson of being "blazingly naive and willfully naive" about authoritarian leaders.

"We're now less than a month away from Election Day, and Tucker Carlson decided, what do you want to do right before Election Day?" Cruz asked rhetorically.

Special: Did You See the VA Benefits You Might Be Missing Out On?

Cruz continued: "I know, become a full-on Nazi. Embrace Adolf Hitler, defend the Nazis, argue America should have been standing with the Nazis. You know, poor Adolf was just misunderstood. We're going to come with the receipts of even for Tucker, long after he's gone down the road of hating Donald Trump, long after he's gone down the road of hating Israel and Jews, long after he's gone down the road of hating Christian Zionists, and becoming a full-on jihadist, long after he has embraced Abdul El-Sayed, Tucker decided, you know, I don't have enough Nazi love on my show, and this past week he sought to correct that. You can hear and judge for yourself."

The Texas Republican also attacked Carlson over a separate portion of the Rees-Mogg interview in which Carlson asserted that Russia has a "much larger economy" than Britain.

Rees-Mogg disputed the claim, arguing Russia has a smaller economy despite its larger population and resources.

"Tucker has an ideological mission," Cruz charged. "It is a mission to tear down America, to tear down free enterprise, to tear down the Constitution."
https://t.co/A3j06FdbLE
Cruz escalated his criticism further, saying Carlson's rhetoric serves to "build up the Nazis" and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Later, discussing Carlson's criticism of Britain's wartime detention of fascist leader Oswald Mosley and others, Cruz declared: "Tucker is all in on defending the Nazis against the West."

Cruz concluded that Carlson's rhetoric was "profoundly dangerous," urging listeners to judge the commentator by his own words.

"You don't have to take my word for it," Cruz said, "because you can listen in his own words as we played today."

‘We Want Islam For This Country’: Muslims In Texas Lay Out Vision For Islamic America
Act for AmericaOct 6📷 📷📷📷📷
By: Joshua Monnington
The organization hosting the event has plans for a 40,000-square-foot Islamic facility near Plano, Texas.
Shaykh Uthman ibn Farooq laid out a vision for an Islamic America during a livestreamed event at the Sufaraa Center in McKinney, Texas, last week. Authentic Ilm Mission, which hosted the event, has plans for a 40,000-square-foot facility near Plano, Texas, and used the livestream featuring Farooq to fundraise for the multipurpose school and Islamic community center.

“We love this country,” Farooq said. “We want good for this country. And that’s why we want Islam for this country, ’cause we think that’s the best thing. And we’re not going to be ashamed of that.”

He went on to argue that Muslims are fully within their constitutional rights to adhere to Sharia law. “We’re Muslims. That’s our identity, and there’s nothing wrong with that. The Constitution of this country protects that. That’s our right to believe in the Sharia. Yes, I said it. That’s our right.”
“There’s communists that believe in communism and live in America,” Farooq continued. “The current mayor of New York is a socialist. Bernie Sanders is open socialist. … Our president — I don’t know what the, what he is actually. I don’t think he knows what he is. … But he has that right according to the Constitution. … There are Satanists. There’s a church of Satan. I’ve debated them.”
Farooq works with the One Message Foundation and is a viral social media influencer. His Instagram and YouTube pages boast 430,000 and 1.4 million followers, respectively. The One Message Foundation’s homepage says it, together with other groups, converted nearly 1,500 individuals to Islam during the World Cup. Farooq’s social media videos feature his commentary speaking of polygamy as legitimate and speculating that President Donald Trump may be an evil spirit.

The event host, Authentic Ilm Mission (AIM), which is led by Dr. Karim AbuZaid and Farooq, is fundraising for an expansive Islamic facility “in one of the most densely Muslim-populated areas between Richardson and Plano,” according to the group’s website. On the former site of a Christian church, the four-acre campus and its facilities — 40,000 square feet in total — will be used to host “Islamic K-12 education,” a seminary, and training in Da’wah, that is, Islamic proselytization.

The AIM website describes the project as having raised $300,000 of the $800,000 needed, with donations reportedly coming from 1,500 individuals in 50 countries. The site features a video of a mosque displacing a beautiful church building with a steeple and classical brick architecture. A different graphic on the website allows users to swipe across the screen to replace an image of the church building at the address listed with an image of the new mosque. The number of mosques in America has surpassed 3,000 in recent years.

During the livestreamed event, Farooq said that the classes offered at the “Da’wah center” would help “educate our youth to have that knowledge … [and] refute Christian apologists and Islamophobes and hadith-rejectors and anybody else that’s trying to deviate Islam.”

He also warned against compromising Islamic principles, framing the warning in terms of Muslims’ military conquests in Europe. Muslims being driven out of parts of Europe in and around the 1500s demonstrate the consequences of compromise, Farooq said: “Portugal and Spain, Sicily — these areas were under Muslim rule for around 700 years. … When the Muslims went there, one of the leaders of the Muslims … went with sword in hand, iman in heart … The Quran was on their tongues. It was in their hearts. It was in their actions. And Allah made them victorious. Victory after victory until, to the middle of Europe, they were victorious. Seven hundred years of compromise, of trying to accommodate ended with what? the Muslims losing.”

Farooq is no stranger to controversy. Yvette Cooper, who was serving as home secretary at the time, barred Farooq from visiting the United Kingdom due to comments justifying Muslims having sex with female captives, a position endorsed by Muhammad in the Quran. Farooq visited Europe in April 2025. When speaking at a Birmingham mosque, he said, “The future is ours. Every ideal nightmare of a Muslim Europe will come true.”

Texas has one of the highest Muslim populations in the United States at more than 300,000, and a significant portion resides in the Dallas-Fort Worth area. The intended site for the Authentic Ilm Mission facility is situated about 20 minutes southwest of the East Plano Islamic Center (EPIC) mosque, which boasts 10,000 members and is embroiled in controversy that garnered nationwide attention with its efforts to establish a Muslim city. The legal battle over EPIC’s planned complex of more than 450 housing plots is ongoing.

While British police have arrested several suspects linked to the conspiracy, the Pentagon's decision to physically withdraw its premiere long-range strike platforms highlights a profound vulnerability in continental defense infrastructure against low-cost, deniable aerial threats.**

GEOPOLITICAL IMPLICATIONS:

The disruption of US bomber operations in the United Kingdom reveals that Western strategic bases are no longer sanctuary zones.

Historically, continental Europe offered secure rear-guard staging areas where advanced weaponry could be serviced without risk.

This logistical security is now obsolete as foreign adversaries deploy asymmetric strike technologies directly to the British heartland.

The relocation of strategic assets demonstrates that physical distance from active war zones no longer guarantees operational safety.

By forcing the relocation of B-1B Lancers, Tehran has demonstrated that it can achieve strategic denial without firing a shot.

This tactical success relies on the use of deniable, low-cost drone capabilities that exploit gaps in domestic civil-military airspace.

Using localized agents, hostile states can execute surveillance, harassment, and kinetic sabotage against highly fortified installations.

This method bypasses traditional air defense systems, which are designed to detect incoming ballistic missiles rather than low-flying drones.

The threat profile has shifted from passive espionage to active operational disruption and potential kinetic damage on NATO territory.

The swift response of British counter-terrorism units indicates that the plot was in an advanced stage of planning and execution.

• The United States Air Force deployed B-1B bombers to RAF Fairford as part of a scheduled Bomber Task Force mission.

• British police arrested several suspects in their 20s, highlighting the recruitment of localized operators for sensitive sabotage plots.

• A single B-1B Lancer costs approximately eighty-five million dollars, creating a highly asymmetrical risk-to-reward ratio for hostile actors.

• The B-1B carries a massive payload of precision-guided munitions, making it a critical asset for NATO's global rapid-strike posture.

This integration of foreign intelligence assets with domestic actors creates a complex, hard-to-detect security threat for security services.

The strategic implications of this evacuation ripple across the entire NATO command structure and alter forward deployment doctrines.

Air Force planners must now assume that any forward-deployed asset in Western Europe is vulnerable to synchronized sabotage campaigns.

This realization will likely accelerate the development of active defense systems around critical military installations in Europe.

Furthermore, it complicates the defense of the eastern flank, which relies heavily on Western European bases for rapid reinforcement.

The incident also highlights the growing sophistication of Iranian intelligence operations outside the Middle East theater of operations.

Tehran is proving capable of projecting threat vectors directly into the domestic space of key permanent UN Security Council members.

This represents a calculated challenge to Western deterrence, gambling that domestic sabotage will not trigger a direct state-on-state response.

SYSTEMIC IMPACT:

The relocation of US strategic assets under direct threat from non-state and state-sponsored asymmetric actors signals a fundamental shift.

The era of uncontested airspace and secure rear-area logistics in Europe has officially ended.

As peer competitors observe this vulnerability, the reliance on forward-deployed heavy bombers will increasingly become a liability.

This dynamic forces Western militaries to accelerate the dispersion of forces and invest heavily in localized air defenses.

It also signals a shift in global deterrence where high-tech conventional supremacy is neutralized by low-tech asymmetric denial.

The long-term balance of power is tilting toward actors who can project disruption cheaply, undermining traditional military hegemony.

Ultimately, this forces a reallocation of resources away from offensive force projection toward defensive domestic securing of critical bases.

text:
girl i went out with recently told me she goes on dates with guys she doesn't like for "anthropological study". she said she went out with a cowboy once just to see what he was like

we met at a friend's birthday picnic. she was wearing a floral green dress. i don't like chatting in groups much so we didn't talk a lot. we walked to the tube with the others after. when the sun set the picnic ended so it was getting darker and darker as we walked

she mentioned she was moving soon. it was coincidentally very close to where i live. i said we should get coffee sometime. i meant it. she agreed. i gave her my phone number but didn't actually get hers. i didn't hear from her for a while

a few weeks later i got an unexpected message from an unknown number. it was a screenshot of my face on a dating app. i was a bit creeped out at first but settled down when i realised it was her

she first asked me if i wanted to do a hackathon together. from what little i knew of her, she'd studied law and was a workaholic, i said no. hackathons aren't my thing and it seemed like a lot of work

after i declined i didn't hear from her for a few days but then she asked me last minute if i wanted to grab dinner. she was feeling sichuan food, intestines to be exact. i told her i knew a place that was very authentic but it was an hour away

"hell no" she said. "there's one 5 minutes from my place"

i knew the only reason she was texting me was because i was available and lived walking distance from her place and i knew the only reason i was going was because i'd eaten too many meals alone lately

she told me to give her an hour to decide. she was feeling a bit sick and might pull out last minute. i wasn't sure if she was telling the truth but 45 minutes into the hour i started walking. i was wearing my nice new denim jacket and i'd waxed my hair. i had a feeling she'd be fine and wouldn't stand me up. i got there first and she arrived a few minutes after

pig intestines were on the menu as she knew they would be. she asked what else we should get. i suggested some vegetables to balance the meal. she suggested something complicated that she couldn't cook at home easily. she ordered in flawless chinese. i stayed silent wondering if i could have ordered in my broken chinese

we talked about london as we waited, how long we'd been here, which parts we liked. we were feeling each other out. i took a lot of small sips of water. she had beautiful brown eyes that kept gazing at me like i was food

the real food arrived not long after. we didn't talk much as we ate. i said it was nice, spicy but not too spicy. she said it was oily and she'd had better. it had a satisfying crunch but it was too spicy for me. i'd never order it myself but i enjoyed it with her. i topped up her water when it was half full and she said thank you every time

as the food slowly disappeared she asked me if there was anything i wanted to ask her. she flashed her teeth. i smiled and looked away. there was a sign for karaoke on the wall. i asked her if she liked karaoke. she said it was okay. she preferred listening to others sing

the bill came and we both knew it would be split. my card declined twice. i had cash too but used my backup card instead since i didn't want to complicate things. we left with her leading the way

outside the restaurant she told me i walk like a guy who's done a lot of tai chi. it was the nicest thing she said to me all night

neither of us wanted to go home yet. there was a big shopping centre next to us so we walked around outside. most of the shops were closed, shutters down, cleaners cleaning. there were still a decent amount of people out, eating in restaurants, drinking in bars

we chatted about her job as a lawyer being ai proof, about my past tech job, about how ironic it was that ai was going to take over so many tech jobs. polite conversation for polite people

we ended up in an arcade. she said she passed it every day on her way to work and always wanted to go in but never had time. we were only going in to look but i had a feeling we were going to end up playing something

i tried hard to remember which ones caught her eye so we could go back to them. at the end of the arcade there were token machines so i suggested we get some

the only game we ended up playing was a horse riding game. the horses were well painted, the seats were sturdy, and there were flashing neon lights on the front and sides. we wanted to play multiplayer since there were two horses side by side but it didn't work out so we took turns: me first and then her. we both kinda sucked. she had a ponytail that matched the horse's tail and she gripped the reins hard as it vibrated. i got a video of her riding the horse. she looked very pleased

the arcade was closing so we got ice cream at a burger place. she wanted one with bacon in it but the guy at the counter said they didn't do that anymore

"we can't have anything nice these days because of woke"

we shared a small ice cream while she ranted about rationalism. she said she just couldn't read that many blog posts. i tried to eat less and save her some but she insisted i eat more of it. she wanted to watch her figure

it was getting late so we walked to near where she lived. there were benches nearby so we sat. it was getting chillier and a fox wandered past

you'd think we'd run out of things to say but we never did. she told me, "conversation is easy. you just say stuff." i agreed. we talked about things we'd done recently. i mentioned i went to a dance class. she asked me to show her what i learned so we started dancing. she'd never danced before and i had just one lesson under my belt so it was very mechanical. there was no music to dance to. she was hard to lead. or i was a bad leader

after our little dance, i showed her some tai chi which she found amusing

"why is a young guy like you doing tai chi?"

"preparing for the future"

i wanted to show her how sturdy tai chi can make you but i didn't want to push her onto the pavement so she suggested we go back to her place. we were right outside. i asked her if her housemates were around and she said all but one should be away. it was a very modern flat. everything looked new

we sat on the sofa next to each other. we started talking about what it's like to date in a big city. she'd lived here for almost a decade. she showed me her hinge profile. she had hundreds of matches. she complained about how all the good boys must be locked behind a paywall. she didn't want to pay

her profile was alright but nothing special. i thought i could have picked out better photos for her. none of them looked like her on the horse. she pointed at a photo of her with a guy and said it was her best friend back home

"at one point my friends and family thought we were meant for each other"

it was almost like we were at confession and i was the priest. this is what i imagine confession is like

she told me she went on dates with guys she didn't even like. "anthropological study," she called it. one time there was a cowboy. she went out with him just to see what he was like. he had the hat and the boots and the ranch and all. she showed me pictures of him on her dating app, at the rodeo, riding a horse, being american. he had big bright white teeth which he flashed in every photo. she scrolled through them proudly as if he was a stamp she'd collected

she said for her bachelorette party she wanted a cowboy theme, at a ranch, with everyone dressed as cowboys. she wasn't joking. i thought it was funny that one cowboy had left such a mark on her

then i realised i was the cowboy this time

i excused myself to go to the bathroom. it was 3am. i wondered what i should do. i could go home but i'd passed the stage where i was tired and wanted to sleep. my sleep schedule was already ruined so it didn't matter when i slept now. the bathroom was clean but not too clean. there were products scattered everywhere. it was definitely an all girls bathroom. i looked at myself in the mirror for a while. my eyes were red

i came out and we chatted some more. at this stage it was mostly her talking and me listening and making comments here and there. i was ok with it. she was ok with it. it was an ideal situation. she was a natural born talker and i was a natural born listener so we had a good thing going on

we talked about dating again. she was a lawyer so maybe it made sense that she found relationship contracts romantic. forget chocolates or flowers. she wanted a contract

"hey maybe we could make a—" she cut herself off. or maybe i interrupted her. i can't remember

she asked me "is there something wrong with me?"

she loved going on first dates and never talking to the guy again. something about being entertained by a different guy each time was thrilling. she was living different lives. she'd never gotten attached to anyone, and if she had, it ended very soon. she'd never been in a long relationship. she asked me what it was like. i was the expert apparently. i tried to reassure her there was nothing wrong with her

it was 6am. we'd talked all night. she offered for me to stay over. i declined the spare mattress and the sofa and her lovely company. i wanted to sleep in my own bed that night

i didn't take the tube. it took a while to get home. it got lighter and lighter as i walked. the birds were already up. it was a good night

the next day i sent her the video of her riding the horse. no caption or anything. i just wanted her to have it too

the day after i sent her one last message not expecting a reply. i never heard from her again

Fact check. 
Hind sight is 20/20 and 
an impartial teacher for those willing to learn.

📷📷📷20 sources

Thought for 20s

The post's central claim 
needs a factual check 
before any lecture can rest on it. 

I'll look up 
the Army benzodiazepine / PTSD evidence 
and the surrounding literature, 
then build the lecture 
and the poem from what holds up.

Thought
A seminar lecture, 
then the poem. 

The Facebook note of 6 October 2020 
is the provocation. 

The record underneath 
it is narrower than the note, 
and the lecture is written 
to that difference.

On the ban 
that was not quite a ban, 
and the collapse that did not quite come

Graduate seminar. 

Law, 
political science, 
medicine,
 social anthropology. 

The text 
on the table
 is a private post 
from six years ago today: 
ban Xanax, 
ban Ambien, 
ban the addicting medicines 
used for chronic mental illness, 
and watch 
revenue streams collapse t
ogether with addiction 
and post-traumatic stress disorder. 

Hindsight, the author says,
 is an impartial teacher. 

The back story offered with 
it is sharper still: 
the United States Army 
banned benzodiazepines 
for acute stress 
because they increased PTSD 
by 500 percent.T

ake the back story first,
 because a lecture 
that begins in a number 
has to know what the number is.

In April 2012 
the Army Medical Command i
ssued a policy memorandum 
on the diagnosis and treatment of PTSD. 

Benzodiazepines 
— alprazolam (Xanax), 
diazepam (Valium), 
and their class 
— were to be treated as 
relatively contraindicated i
n combat veterans. 

The stated reasons 
were not a single trial result. 

They were comorbidity 
with alcohol and substance use, 
often approaching half of cases; 
tolerance and dependence 
that made discontinuation 
very difficult; 
and clinical observation 
that the drugs
 could intensify 
rather than settle combat stress.

A contemporaneous review 
by Jolene Bostwick 
put the prevention claim plainly: 
benzodiazepine administration 
fails to prevent PTSD 
and may increase its incidence. 

The 2023 VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline 
now strongly recommends 
against benzodiazepines 
for PTSD 
and acute stress disorder. 

The American Psychological Association does the same.

VA prescribing of benzodiazepines t
o veterans 
with PTSD 
fell from about 
31 percent in 2009 to about 
11 percent in 2019. 

That is a real institutional reversal. 

It is not a ban, 
and it is not a finding
 of a 500 percent increase.

The quantitative literature
 is messier than the slogan. 

A 2015 systematic review 
(Guina and colleagues, 
Journal of Psychiatric Practice) 
concluded that benzodiazepines 
are ineffective 
for treatment 
and prevention of PTSD, 
and that studies with usable data
 suggested a two- to five-fold 
higher risk of developing PTSD 
when the drugs 
were given after recent trauma 
— an upper bound 
that can be spoken, 
loosely, as a 400 percent increase, 
which is where “500 percent” comes from. 

A 2022 meta-analysis 
of the prevention literature 
found a risk ratio of about 
1.53 in cohort studies, 
with a confidence interval 
that just clears 1, 
and judged the underlying studies 
poor to moderate in quality. 
One often-cited comparison 
— 63 percent meeting PTSD criteria 
at six months on
 a benzodiazepine versus 
23 percent on placebo 
— is roughly a 2.7-fold difference, 
from a small early trial. 

A large 2026 naturalistic study
 after the 7 October attacks
found no increased twelve-month PTSD risk 
from short-term new benzodiazepine use, 
and an elevated risk 
only among persistent users. 

The honest summary
 for a methods seminar is this: 
early and especially 
continued benzodiazepine use 
after trauma 
is associated 
with worse PTSD outcomes 
and is no longer recommended; 
the magnitude 
is not a settled 500 percent; 
confounding by indication 
has never been fully retired, 
because the most distressed patients 
are the ones who receive the drug.

Ambien belongs in a different sentence. 

Zolpidem is a Z-drug, 
not a benzodiazepine, 
though it binds 
the same GABA-A receptor family 
and carries 
dependence, 
complex sleep behaviors, 
and withdrawal of its own. 

It is not the drug 
named in the 2012 Army memorandum. 

Folding it into the same prohibition 
is a rhetorical move, 
not a guideline.

With the number corrected,
 the post’s larger claim 
can be taught.

Medicine
Benzodiazepines are true anxiolytics. 
They work within minutes 
because they potentiate GABA, t
he principal inhibitory transmitter. 

That is why 
they are still used 
for alcohol withdrawal, 
status epilepticus, 
procedural sedation, 
and severe acute agitation. 

It is also
 why they are a poor instrument
 for the biology of PTSD.

PTSD 
is not simply too much fear. 

It is a disorder 
of memory consolidation, 
extinction learning, 
and hyperarousal
 in which 
cortisol dynamics, 
norepinephrine, 
and fear-circuit plasticity 
all matter. 

A drug 
that blunts the acute affective peak 
can also blunt 
the encoding 
and the later reconsolidation 
that extinction therapies 
rely on. 

Prolonged exposure, 
in one trial, 
produced less symptom reduction 
when paired with alprazolam 
than when given alone. 

Patients describe the same thing 
without the vocabulary: 
the feeling is gone, 
the memory is not, 
and the capacity t
o sit with the memory atrophies. 

Chronic use adds 
tolerance, 
withdrawal 
anxiety that mimics the original illness, 
cognitive dulling, 
falls in older adults, 
and 
— in a large VA cohort
 — higher health-care use 
and a markedly higher
 hazard of suicide attempt 
and suicide death. 

Association is not proof of causation. 

It is enough, 
with the failure of efficacy trials, 
for every major guideline 
to recommend against.

What the post overreaches i
s the prediction 
that the syndromes themselves 
would collapse 
if the drugs were withdrawn. 

PTSD has a trauma etiology 
and a natural history 
that predates alprazolam 
(approved 1981) 
and the modern DSM category 
(1980). 

First-line care in the current guideline i
s trauma-focused psychotherapy 
— prolonged exposure, 
cognitive processing therapy, 
EMDR 
— and, if medication is used, 
sertraline, 
paroxetine, 
or venlafaxine. 

Those are not revenue-free. 
They are also not benzodiazepines. 

A ban on Xanax 
would not retire the diagnosis.

 It would retire one iatrogenic amplifier 
and one dependence market.

Law
The legal questions sit one level up from the prescription pad.Informed consent. 

A service member 
or a veteran 
handed a benzodiazepine 
for acute combat stress
 in 2006 
was often 
not told that t
he same institution 
would later call the drug 
relatively contraindicated, 
nor that early use 
might raise the probability 
of the chronic disorder. 

Doctrine of informed consent 
assumes a stable knowledge base. 

Here the knowledge base moved. 

That is a problem 
for malpractice timelines, 
for the Feres doctrine’s 
bar on suits by active-duty members
 against the government, 
and for VA disability claims 
in which the treatment 
and the condition are entangled.

Regulatory classification. 
Alprazolam and zolpidem 
are Schedule IV controlled substances. 

The scheduling
 already concedes abuse potential.
 It does not concede t
hat the labeled indications 
are fictitious, 
and it does not authorize 
a clinician, 
a board, 
or a lecture 
to “ban” them by manifesto. 

A real ban 
would be a scheduling action, 
a label withdrawal, 
or a coverage determination. 

Each has a statutory path
 — FDA, DEA, CMS, the VA formulary 
— and each 
has already been walked partway 
by guideline 
and by the VA’s own prescribing decline.

Liability the other direction. 
Once a guideline 
strongly recommends against a drug, 
continued routine use 
becomes the exposure. 

The WSJ’s 2025 reporting 
on the “combat cocktail” 
— veterans maintained for years 
on simultaneous CNS drugs 
despite VA guidance 
that combinations lack supporting data 
— is the factual predicate 
for that exposure. 

Law students 
should notice who the defendant would be: 
not only the manufacturer, 
but the system 
that kept writing the prescriptions 
after its own document said not to.

Political science

The revenue claim 
is the part the post wants believed, 
and it is half right.

Psychotropic prescribing 
to active-duty troops rose several-fold 
across the Iraq and Afghanistan wars. 

Antipsychotics, 
which the Army also cautioned against 
for PTSD in that 2012 memo,
rose fastest. 

Benzodiazepine prescriptions 
in the force rose 
on the order of several hundred percent 
in the same window. 

The VA, 
against its own advice, 
continued to dispense benzodiazepines 
to a very large number of patients 
with PTSD well after 2004–2005 signals. 

Polypharmacy
— the cocktail 
— became common:
 nearly 60 percent of VA PTSD patients 
on two or more CNS drugs 
by 2019 
in the figures reported from VA data. 

Manufacturers of on-patent drugs 
had an interest in the expansion. 

So did a personnel system 
that needed symptomatic soldiers returned to duty, 
and a clinical culture 
that had a pill for sleeplessness
 and a thin supply of psychotherapists.

That is a political economy of overtreatment. 
It is not evidence that PTSD 
or addiction are artifacts 
invented to protect the revenue. 

The same decades 
produced a large,
 ugly epidemiologic signal 
— more psychiatric prescribing, 
more suicide in the force 
than in some periods of combat, 
dependence layered on trauma. 

Incentives explain the speed and the excess. 

They do not explain the index trauma, 
and they do not predict 
that the syndromes vanish 
when one drug class is restricted. 

The prescribing of benzodiazepines 
did fall, sharply, 
after the guidelines hardened. 

PTSD caseloads did not collapse with them. 

New drug classes 
moved into the space 
the benzodiazepines left. 

Students of regulation 
should treat that substitution as the finding.

Social anthropology

The diagnosis is also a social fact

.PTSD as a named entity is young. 
Its inclusion in DSM-III 
was in part a victory for Vietnam veterans 
and their clinicians, 
who needed a category 
that located the injury 
in the event rather 
than in a weak character. 

The category then traveled. 
It medicalized responses to 
combat, 
rape, 
disaster, 
and, later, 
a widening set of adversities. 

Anthropologists have argued 
for forty years 
about what was gained 
and what was lost:
 recognition and care on one side; 
the export of a Western disease model, 
the thinning of local idioms of distress, 
and the capture of suffering 
by a pharmacy on the other.

Benzodiazepines sit inside that argument 
as a technology of quieting. T

hey do not require a narrative. 

They do not require a witness. 

In a garrison, 
a clinic, 
or a household, 
they convert an unspeakable state 
into a manageable one 
for the length of a half-life. 

The Army’s later reversal 
is interesting anthropologically 
because the institution 
that had used the technology 
to keep manpower available d
eclared that the technology 
was making the illness worse 
and the soldier harder to separate 
from the drug. 

“Hindsight is 20/20” 
is the folk version of that reversal. 

It is not impartial. 

Hindsight in medicine 
is produced by committees, 
meta-analyses, 
scandal, 
and the accumulation of bodies. 

It is a teacher 
only for those 
who can tolerate a revision 
of what they were told was care.

The post’s moral 
— ban the drug and watch the illness fall 
— reverses the usual medicalization critique.

 Instead of saying the diagnosis 
created the market,
 it says the market sustains the diagnosis.

 Both can be true in part. 
Neither is the whole mechanism. 

Addiction to the drug is real 
and iatrogenic in a straightforward way. 

PTSD as a human response 
to overwhelming threat
 is older than the patent.

What a seminar can carry out of the room

The 2012 memorandum 
and the 2023 guideline 
are the part of the post 
that survives contact 
with the literature. 

Benzodiazepines after trauma 
are a bad prevention strategy 
and a poor treatment; 
dependence is common; 
guidelines have already moved; 
practice has moved 
more slowly than the documents. 

The 500 percent figure 
is an upper-bound slogan, 
not an Army result. 

Ambien is a cousin, 
not the same case. 

The predicted collapse of PTSD 
and of addiction, 
upon a ban, 
is not a finding 
and not a responsible forecast. 

The predicted pressure 
on revenue 
is the part worth keeping, 
as a question about substitution: 
when one stream is closed, 
where does the next prescription come from, 
and who is still symptomatic 
when it arrives.

Hindsight is a teacher. 
It is not an impartial one.
 It arrives late, 
it arrives unevenly, 
and it is only as good 
as the distinction 
it can still draw 
between a drug 
that quiets a night 
and a drug 
that writes the next year 
of the illness.

Money (after the remaster)
In 7/4, cash-register cynicism, 
for the seminar that stayed late.

Money, get away. 
Get a good script 
with more refills
and you’re okay. 
Money, it’s a gas. 
Grab that tab 
with both hands 
and make a stash. 
New script, 
brand-new fear, 
four-star daydream, 
Think I’ll buy me 
a quiet regime
.Money, get back.
 I’m all right, Jack, 
keep your hands off my stack. 
Money, it’s a hit. 
Don’t give me 
that do-goody-good bullshit.
 I’m in the high-fidelity
 first-class traveling set, 
And I think
I need 
another Xanax yet.
New war, 
old pill, 
half-life daydream, 
Army says it feeds 
the thing it treats. 
Two times,
 five times, 
somebody shouted five, 
Hindsight cashes the check 
and stays alive. 
Guideline, formulary, 
strongly-against machine, 
Think I’ll buy me 
a different stream.
Money, it’s a crime. 
Share it fairly, 
but don’t take
 a slice of my pie. 
Money, so they say, 
Is the root of all evil today. 
But if you ask 
for a rise 
it’s no surprise 
That they’re giving none away, 
away, away. Away, 
ban the bottle, 
watch the tower fall 
— Down, down, down, down. 
Diagnosis doesn’t fall. 
It learns to crawl 
To the next name 
on the pad, 
the next receipt,
 The next soft mouth 
of a revenue stream. 
Zolpidem dreams. 
Alprazolam days. 
Nobody bans a market. 
It changes shape.
Money, get away. 
You get a good job with more pay 
and you’re okay. 
Money, it’s a gas. 
Grab that cash with both hands 
and make a stash. 
New car, caviar, 
four-star daydream, 
Think I’ll buy me a football team.

text:
The 101st Airborne Division patch, the black Screaming Eagle on a yellow shield, is one of the most recognized and respected combat patches in the Army. Soldiers often call it coveted because it marks service with a unit that has a long record of airborne and air-assault operations, from Normandy and Bastogne in World War II through Vietnam and later deployments in Iraq and Afghanistan.

It is worn as a shoulder sleeve insignia. The version on the left sleeve shows current assignment. The one on the right sleeve is the combat patch, earned only by serving with the division or an attached unit in a designated combat zone. Receiving that right-shoulder patch is a formal mark that the wearer was there during operations, which is why it carries weight inside the formation.

On the evening of January 2nd 2011 in Afghanistan after bringing in a new year I led the group in the mayor cell, the same day word came that Dick Winters had died on a cold January day in Hershey Pennsylvania. A hometown hero, talking about the officer whose Easy Company service helped make the Screaming Eagle famous. Winters himself wore it through Normandy, Market Garden, and the Battle of the Bulge. For many who later served with the division, the patch is a direct link to that history and to leaders like him. Always remember.

The mayor took his patch off and slapped it on my right shoulder. No write up. I’m just a squid. Surrounded by the best that the Army had to offer was enough for me. I knew it and that is why I kept coming back. You could tell. They gave a shit.
